title: FIFA Insider Blows Whistle: Staff 'Deceived' Over Infantino's $20B World Cup Sell-Off
summary:
A stunning revolt is shaking FIFA from the inside. Kevin Lamour, the organization's Chief Operating Officer, has publicly accused President Gianni Infantino of deceiving his own staff over a controversial plan to sell a piece of the World Cup's future earnings to private equity.

In a statement to The Associated Press, Lamour said colleagues were "deceived" by Infantino's lack of transparency and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation." He called the $20 billion proposal "the project of one person" and urged football's political leaders to "ask themselves the right questions."

Hours earlier, Carlos Cordeiro, Infantino's senior adviser and a former Goldman Sachs banker, resigned. Cordeiro, who also served on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, said he was excluded from talks with a New York investment fund created by Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner. "I oppose it unequivocally," he said. "It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification."

The plan would spin off FIFA's commercial businesses—including men's and women's World Cups—into a $20 billion subsidiary, with 20% owned by private investors. Kushner's fund is the "anchor investor." Infantino is offering FIFA's 211 member federations $20 million each to approve the deal by September 19.

Cordeiro, who spent 35 years in banking, argued the math doesn't add up. FIFA already sits on billions in reserves and just earned $15 billion from the recent men's World Cup. Selling a permanent stake to raise $4.2 billion, he said, "makes little sense."

Lamour, who has worked alongside Infantino since his surprise election in 2016, stopped short of resigning but said he had a duty to his colleagues. Both men are calling on other FIFA staff to speak out. With Infantino seemingly unopposed for re-election next March, this internal rebellion could be the biggest challenge yet to his decade-long reign.
why_it_matters: When the people running a global institution like FIFA are accused of hiding the truth about a huge financial deal, it affects who profits from the world’s most popular sport and whether the game’s future is sold to the highest bidder — lessons that apply to any powerful organisation.

background_read: FIFA, the global governing body for football, has a long history of controversy. In 2015, a massive corruption scandal led to the indictment of dozens of officials — the biggest crisis in the organisation’s history. Gianni Infantino was elected president in 2016 on a promise to clean up the institution. His surprise win came after the downfall of Sepp Blatter, the long-serving president who was banned from the sport.

The current revolt centres on a plan to spin off World Cup commercial rights into a $20 billion subsidiary, with a 20% stake sold to private investors. The anchor investor is a fund created by Joshua Kushner — brother of Jared Kushner, who was a senior White House adviser during the Trump administration. This family connection has drawn extra scrutiny to the deal.

Carlos Cordeiro, the former president of the U.S. Soccer Federation and a former Goldman Sachs banker, resigned as Infantino’s adviser in protest. He argued that FIFA already has billions in reserves and just earned $15 billion from the recent men’s World Cup, so selling a permanent share of future earnings for $4.2 billion made little financial sense.

Kevin Lamour, FIFA’s Chief Operating Officer, has not resigned but went public with his accusation of deception, urging other staff to speak out. This rare internal rebellion breaks the culture of silence FIFA is known for, and with Infantino apparently unopposed for re-election next March, it could be the most visible test of his decade-long leadership.

perspectives.description: Proponents argue that an immediate $4.2 billion cash injection could help smaller football federations develop facilities and programmes, especially in poorer regions where FIFA’s development grants are often the main source of funding for grassroots football.

Opponents say the deal mortgages future generations of football. Since private equity investors expect high returns, more World Cup revenues would flow to wealthy investors instead of being reinvested in the sport, potentially driving up ticket prices and commercialisation.

This crisis fits a historical pattern where FIFA presidents face little internal challenge until a major financial decision triggers a rupture. Similar dynamics have played out in the IOC and other international sports bodies, where a mix of lifetime appointments and large sums of money create concentrated power with few checks.

The rebellion could force FIFA to disclose more details of the deal or even trigger a delay in the approval vote. Some observers believe this open dissent might encourage football associations to demand better terms or push for an independent audit, possibly reshaping the governance of the World Cup for decades.
